text: There is a fundamental shift happening in software engineering. For decades, we have been improving the way software is developed. We moved from waterfall methodologies to Agile. We embraced DevOps, automated build and deployment pipelines, introduced infrastructure as code, and invested heavily in developer productivity. Each evolution helped us deliver software faster, more reliably, and with greater consistency. Now, artificial intelligence is introducing another dimension to this evolution. Developers are using AI coding assistants to generate code, write unit tests, troubleshoot problems, and understand unfamiliar codebases. Architects are experimenting with AI to explore design alternatives. Teams are using AI to translate requirements into technical specifications and automate repetitive engineering activities. The productivity improvements are becoming increasingly difficult to ignore. But I think we are asking the wrong question. Most conversations about AI in software development focus on how much faster developers can write code. We discuss code generation, AI copilots, autonomous agents, and productivity gains. What we discuss considerably less is whether the way we organize and execute software development needs to change altogether. Are we simply adding AI capabilities to an existing Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC), or are we moving towards a fundamentally different approach to building software? This is where the concept of AI-Driven Development Life Cycle (AI-DLC) becomes interesting. And I believe it deserves a much deeper conversation than simply comparing AI-generated code with manually written code. The SDLC: A lifecycle built around human execution The traditional Software Development Life Cycle has served the software industry remarkably well. Regardless of whether an organization follows waterfall, iterative development, Agile, or a hybrid methodology, the underlying engineering activities remain relatively consistent. We identify a business problem, gather requirements, design a solution, develop the software, test it, deploy it, and maintain it. The methodologies may differ, but the fundamental responsibilities remain recognizable. Humans understand the business problem, interpret requirements, make architectural decisions, write code, validate functionality, and coordinate delivery. Over the years, we have optimized these activities. Agile introduced shorter feedback cycles and iterative delivery. DevOps brought development and operations closer together. CI/CD automated much of the build, testing, and deployment process. These were significant improvements. However, even with all these advancements, a considerable amount of engineering work still depends on humans translating information from one activity into another. Business requirements become user stories. User stories become technical designs. Technical designs become implementation tasks. Implementation produces code. Testing validates whether the code satisfies the original requirements. Every transition requires interpretation. And interpretation introduces opportunities for information loss, inconsistencies, and misunderstandings. Think about a seemingly straightforward requirement: "Allow customers to update their delivery address." The requirement sounds simple. But an engineer needs to understand the customer domain, authentication model, address validation rules, order lifecycle, downstream integrations, data privacy requirements, and potential impacts on existing functionality. A Jira ticket alone rarely captures all this information. The developer must find the relevant documentation, speak to architects or business analysts, understand existing implementation patterns, and make several engineering decisions before writing code. This is not necessarily a problem with SDLC. It is simply how software engineering has evolved around human capabilities and collaboration. But what happens when AI can participate in these activities? AI-assisted SDLC: Making the existing lifecycle faster The first wave of AI adoption in software engineering has largely focused on improving individual activities within the existing development lifecycle. Developers use AI coding assistants. Test engineers generate test cases using AI. Architects use AI to explore design alternatives. Business analysts use AI to summarize requirements and produce documentation. These capabilities are valuable. However, the fundamental development workflow often remains unchanged. We still have requirements, design, development, testing, and deployment. AI simply helps humans perform some of these activities faster. Consider the difference: A developer receives a Jira story, opens an AI coding assistant, provides the relevant context, and asks it to implement the required functionality. The AI generates code. The developer reviews it, makes corrections, runs tests, and commits the changes. The developer remains responsible for coordinating the entire activity. This is AI-assisted SDLC. It improves productivity, but it does not necessarily change the underlying engineering model. We have introduced a more capable tool into an existing process. I see this as an important transitional phase, but not necessarily the destination. The bigger opportunity is to rethink how these activities are connected and executed. AI-DLC: Rethinking the way software gets built AI-DLC represents a shift in how we approach software development. Instead of introducing AI into individual SDLC activities, we redesign the development lifecycle to make AI an active participant across the engineering process. The starting point is no longer simply a collection of tasks assigned to developers. It is the business intent, the desired outcome, and the constraints within which the solution must operate. Humans define the problem, establish direction, provide business and architectural context, and set boundaries. AI helps transform that intent into structured requirements, specifications, architecture proposals, implementation plans, code, and validation activities. Humans review critical decisions, challenge assumptions, provide direction, and retain accountability for the outcome. The distinction is subtle but important. In AI-assisted SDLC, AI helps us execute existing activities. In AI-DLC, we reconsider how the activities themselves should be structured, coordinated, and executed. I would describe this as moving from AI-assisted tasks to AI-orchestrated engineering workflows. Understanding the three approaches Dimension Traditional SDLC AI-assisted SDLC AI-DLC Starting point Requirements Requirements Business intent Requirements Human-defined AI-assisted AI elaborates, humans validate Planning Human-coordinated AI-supported AI proposes structured plans Architecture Human-led AI-supported Collaborative design and review Development Human implementation AI-assisted coding AI executes bounded engineering tasks Testing Human-designed and automated AI-assisted testing Continuous AI-supported validation Context Documents, tickets, conversations Documents plus AI context Structured and connected engineering context Coordination Human-driven Human-driven with AI support Human-AI orchestration Accountability Human-owned Human-owned Human-owned This comparison is not intended to suggest that every AI-DLC implementation will look identical. AI-DLC is an evolving approach, and different organizations will implement it differently. The important distinction is the underlying philosophy: AI becomes part of the engineering workflow rather than remaining an isolated productivity tool. The real challenge: AI needs engineering context There is one aspect of AI-DLC that I believe deserves particular attention. Context. We often hear that AI models are becoming increasingly capable. Their reasoning, coding, and problem-solving abilities continue to improve. But model capability alone does not guarantee good engineering outcomes. Consider the earlier requirement about updating a customer's delivery address. If an AI agent receives only that sentence, it might generate an API, create a database update operation, and produce a few unit tests. The implementation might even work. But does the agent understand whether an order has already shipped? Can the address be changed after payment? Does the customer need additional verification? Are there downstream systems that need to be notified? What are the organization's API standards? What security controls must be enforced? Without this context, the agent is making assumptions. And assumptions are particularly dangerous when they translate into executable software. This is why I believe AI-DLC needs to be built on a strong foundation of specification-driven development and context engineering. A specification should not merely describe what a feature does. It should capture the business intent, functional requirements, non-functional requirements, constraints, dependencies, acceptance criteria, and relevant architectural decisions. It should also remain connected to the implementation and validation activities that follow. In other words, the specification becomes an engineering asset rather than a document that is created at the beginning of a project and gradually forgotten. Imagine an engineering workflow in which an AI agent can access the relevant Jira stories, Confluence documentation, architecture standards, API contracts, domain models, and existing codebase. It can use this information to propose a solution, identify missing requirements, highlight architectural conflicts, and generate an implementation plan. That is considerably more powerful than asking an AI coding assistant to implement a Jira ticket. The objective is not to give AI access to everything. It is to provide the right context, at the right time, with the appropriate access controls. The lifecycle needs to change, not just the tools If we accept that AI can participate across the engineering lifecycle, we need to reconsider how the lifecycle is organized. I would think about AI-DLC through six interconnected engineering activities. 1. Specify — Establish the intent Start with the business problem rather than immediately translating it into development tasks. AI can help analyze requirements, identify ambiguities, ask clarifying questions, and produce structured specifications. Humans validate the business interpretation and approve the requirements. 2. Plan and architect — Establish the solution AI can analyze the existing architecture, identify dependencies, propose design alternatives, and generate implementation plans. Architects remain responsible for evaluating trade-offs, security, scalability, integration patterns, and architectural alignment. 3. Decompose — Make the work executable The approved solution is translated into smaller, traceable engineering tasks. AI can identify dependencies, suggest task sequencing, and establish the relationship between requirements, designs, and implementation activities. 4. Implement — Execute engineering work AI coding agents work on bounded tasks using approved specifications, architectural context, coding standards, and existing implementation patterns. Developers review the changes, resolve complex problems, and remain accountable for code quality. 5. Validate — Establish correctness AI helps generate and execute tests, analyze failures, review implementation against specifications, and identify potential regressions. Traditional deterministic testing remains essential. AI-generated validation must itself be evaluated rather than blindly trusted. 6. Deliver and learn — Close the engineering loop Validated changes move through established release and deployment controls. Production feedback, defects, performance metrics, and operational observations feed into subsequent engineering decisions. The important point is that these activities should not operate as disconnected stages. They should form a continuous, traceable engineering workflow. Why this is more than an AI coding exercise One concern I have with the current AI development conversation is that we are measuring progress primarily through developer productivity. How much code can an AI agent generate? How many hours can it save? How many developers can a team support? These are useful questions, but they do not adequately measure the maturity of AI-driven software engineering. Consider a team that generates twice as much code using AI but spends significantly more time reviewing, correcting, and maintaining it. Has engineering productivity actually improved? What if the code is generated quickly but does not align with enterprise architecture standards? What if the implementation passes unit tests but violates an important business rule? What if an AI agent introduces a security vulnerability while attempting to solve a functional requirement? Increasing code generation is not the same as increasing software delivery capability. I believe we need to measure AI-DLC through broader engineering outcomes: Time from business intent to validated implementation. Requirement-to-code traceability. Architecture and security compliance. Defect rates and rework. Test effectiveness and coverage. Engineering throughput and delivery predictability. Production reliability and business outcomes. Ultimately, the objective should be better software delivered more effectively, not simply more software delivered faster. What happens to the role of engineers and architects? This is probably one of the most interesting implications of AI-DLC. If AI agents increasingly participate in requirements analysis, planning, coding, testing, and documentation, does that reduce the importance of engineers? I would argue the opposite. It changes where engineering judgment becomes most valuable. Engineers will need to spend less time on repetitive implementation activities and more time understanding business problems, validating assumptions, making design decisions, evaluating trade-offs, and ensuring that systems behave as intended. Architects will need to think beyond producing diagrams and technical documents. They will need to establish the architectural context, constraints, patterns, and decision boundaries within which AI agents operate. Engineering leaders will need to reconsider how teams are organized, how work is assigned, how quality is measured, and how accountability is maintained. This is not about removing engineering expertise from software development. It is about using that expertise differently. The ability to generate code is becoming increasingly accessible. The ability to understand what should be built, why it should be built, how it should fit into a broader system, and whether it is correct will remain critical. My perspective: We should stop optimizing only for faster coding I believe we are approaching an important transition in software engineering. For years, we have optimized the development lifecycle around making human engineering activities more efficient. We introduced better methodologies, development frameworks, automation platforms, and collaboration tools. AI introduces an opportunity to reconsider the entire operating model. But I don't believe the answer is to replace every engineering activity with an autonomous agent. There will always be decisions that require human judgment, business understanding, architectural accountability, and risk assessment. There will also be situations where a simple deterministic implementation is better than introducing an AI model. The real opportunity lies in identifying which activities benefit from AI, which should remain deterministic, and where human approval is essential. AI-DLC should not be viewed as an attempt to eliminate SDLC. The engineering foundations established through decades of software development remain relevant. Architecture, security, testing, version control, deployment automation, and operational excellence are still essential. What needs to change is how we orchestrate these capabilities. The next evolution of software engineering will not be defined by how quickly we can generate code. It will be defined by how effectively we can translate intent into reliable software using human expertise and AI capabilities together. That, to me, is the real promise of AI-DLC. And perhaps the most important question for engineering leaders is no longer how to introduce AI coding assistants into their teams. It is whether their existing software development lifecycle is ready for a fundamentally different way of building software. AI Engineering Series, Part 1: Rethinking the Software Development Lifecycle In the next article: Specification-Driven Development — The Missing Foundation of AI-DLC.

There is something interesting happening in software engineering today. Almost everyone seems to be experimenting with AI. Developers are writing prompts, generating code, building prototypes, connecting APIs to language models, and demonstrating applications that would have taken considerably longer to develop just a few years ago. The barrier to building something with AI has dropped significantly. But I think we are beginning to confuse the ability to build something with AI with the ability to engineer a production-ready AI solution. These are two very different things. Writing a good prompt is a useful skill. Knowing how to get a language model to produce a particular response is valuable. But neither, by itself, makes someone an AI engineer. The real engineering challenge begins when we take that promising prototype and attempt to turn it into something that businesses and customers can depend on. And that is where the conversation needs to change. The illusion of simplicity Consider a relatively straightforward use case: building an AI-powered enterprise knowledge assistant. The requirement sounds simple enough. Employees should be able to ask questions in natural language and receive answers based on internal organizational documents, policies, and knowledge repositories. A typical prototype might involve connecting a language model to a collection of documents, writing a prompt with some instructions, and presenting the response through a chat interface. It works. The demonstration is impressive. People start imagining all the possibilities. But what happens when the application moves beyond a demonstration? What happens when an employee asks a question about a document they are not authorized to access? What happens when the retrieved information is incomplete or outdated? What happens when the model confidently generates an answer that is not supported by the underlying information? What happens when the model provider experiences an outage, response times increase, or token consumption becomes unexpectedly expensive? And perhaps more importantly, how do we establish that the application is consistently producing correct and useful answers? Suddenly, the problem is no longer about writing a better prompt. It becomes a software engineering problem involving architecture, identity, authorization, data quality, integration, observability, resilience, performance, cost management, and governance. This is the distinction I believe we need to recognize. AI can simplify the interaction, but it does not eliminate the engineering complexity underneath it. From prompts to engineered workflows Traditional software engineering is built around predictable execution paths. We define inputs, implement business rules, process data, and produce outputs. There can certainly be complexity, but we generally have considerable control over how the application behaves. AI introduces a different dimension. Language models are probabilistic. The same request can produce different responses. Their outputs can be useful, incomplete, inconsistent, or occasionally incorrect. We cannot approach these systems with the same assumptions we use when designing conventional business applications. Imagine an AI-powered application that processes customer requests. A simplistic implementation might look something like this: Receive a customer request. Send the request to an LLM. Display the generated response. That is a demonstration, not necessarily a production architecture. A more mature implementation needs to understand the customer's identity, retrieve relevant information, apply business rules, determine which tools the model can access, validate the response, and establish whether the result is appropriate for the intended action. The workflow becomes something closer to: Customer Request → Identity & Authorization → Context Retrieval → Model Orchestration → Response Validation → Business Action → Observability Each stage introduces engineering responsibilities. For example, the model might recommend issuing a refund. That does not mean the model should independently execute the transaction. The application must validate the customer's eligibility, check the transaction history, apply refund policies, and enforce the appropriate authorization before allowing the action. The model can help interpret the request and recommend an outcome. The application must retain control over business-critical decisions. This distinction is important. I believe successful AI engineering will increasingly depend on how effectively we combine the flexibility of language models with the predictability and controls of traditional software systems. From individual models to orchestrated systems Another area where I believe our thinking needs to evolve is model selection. There is a tendency to approach AI architecture by asking which language model is the best. I don't think that is the right starting point. The better question is: which model is appropriate for a particular task, considering accuracy, latency, cost, privacy, and operational requirements? Not every interaction needs the most powerful model available. A simple classification request, structured data extraction, summarization task, or intent identification process may not require the same model capabilities as complex reasoning or multi-step problem solving. Using an expensive, high-capability model for every interaction can be an architectural mistake. Consider an enterprise application that handles thousands of requests every day. Some requests might require basic classification. Others might involve retrieving information from multiple systems, interpreting business context, or generating a detailed recommendation. Routing every request through the same model creates unnecessary cost and potentially introduces additional latency. A better architecture introduces model orchestration. The application can identify the nature of the request and select an appropriate model based on the task, available capabilities, performance requirements, and cost constraints. It can also incorporate fallback mechanisms when a particular model or provider becomes unavailable. This is where concepts such as model routing, inference gateways, model abstraction, and provider independence become important. The objective is not to build an unnecessarily complicated AI platform. It is to avoid making the entire application dependent on a single model, provider, or inference strategy. The model should be a component of the architecture, not the architecture itself. From experimentation to production reliability In traditional application engineering, we have spent decades developing practices around availability, scalability, performance, security, and operational excellence. We have monitoring, logging, distributed tracing, deployment automation, disaster recovery, and established reliability practices. AI applications need these foundations too. But they also introduce new dimensions that conventional application monitoring does not adequately address. A service returning HTTP 200 does not necessarily mean the AI application is working correctly. The model may have returned a response, but was the response accurate? Did the retrieval process find the right information? Was the answer grounded in the available context? Did the application expose information that the requesting user should not have accessed? Did the model consume significantly more tokens than expected? Did the response meet the expected latency and quality thresholds? These are fundamentally different questions from simply checking whether an API is available. I believe AI observability needs to evolve beyond infrastructure and application metrics. We need visibility into the complete AI execution lifecycle. That includes: Model performance: Response latency, throughput, failures, and availability. Cost management: Token consumption, inference costs, and cost per successful transaction. Response quality: Accuracy, relevance, groundedness, and evaluation results. Retrieval effectiveness: Whether the right information was retrieved and supplied as context. Security: Identity, authorization, sensitive data exposure, and tool access. Business outcomes: Whether the AI interaction actually helped complete the intended business process. There is an important distinction between a system that successfully invokes a model and a system that consistently delivers business value. We should engineer for the latter. From model accuracy to business outcomes One of the mistakes I see in conversations about AI adoption is the tendency to focus too heavily on the model itself. Organizations discuss which model performs better, which benchmark it scores higher on, or which provider offers the most advanced capabilities. These are useful considerations, but they are not the ultimate measures of success. The real question is whether the solution improves the business process. Consider software engineering productivity. An AI coding assistant might generate code faster. That sounds like a measurable productivity improvement. But what happens if developers spend additional time reviewing incorrect implementations, correcting architectural decisions, fixing security issues, or maintaining code that they do not fully understand? Has productivity actually improved? The answer cannot be determined by counting generated lines of code or measuring how many prompts developers submit. We need to consider the entire engineering lifecycle. Are requirements being translated into better implementations? Is development lead time improving? Are defects increasing or decreasing? Is the quality of code improving? Are developers spending more time solving meaningful engineering problems rather than repetitive tasks? The same principle applies to enterprise AI applications. An AI customer service assistant should not be evaluated simply by how many conversations it handles. We should examine resolution rates, customer satisfaction, escalation rates, accuracy, and the actual cost of serving a customer. AI engineering must connect technical performance to business performance. Otherwise, we risk building impressive technology without solving meaningful problems. From individual productivity to enterprise capability There is another transition that I believe deserves attention. Most organizations begin their AI journey with individual productivity tools. Developers use coding assistants. Business users experiment with copilots. Teams explore document summarization, automated reporting, and conversational interfaces. These are useful starting points. But enterprise adoption requires a broader engineering foundation. How do we establish reusable AI capabilities? How do we standardize model access, authentication, security, and observability? How do we prevent every engineering team from independently building its own model integration, prompt management, and retrieval implementation? How do we establish reusable patterns without restricting teams from experimenting and innovating? This is where I see a natural connection between AI engineering and platform engineering. We have already learned valuable lessons from building internal developer platforms. Standardized deployment pipelines, reusable infrastructure, golden paths, self-service capabilities, and centralized operational visibility help engineering teams build and deliver software more consistently. The same thinking can be applied to AI. Organizations can establish reusable capabilities for model access, inference routing, retrieval, evaluation, security controls, and observability. Teams should not have to solve the same foundational problems repeatedly. At the same time, platform engineering should not become another centralized bottleneck. The objective should be to enable teams to build AI-powered applications faster while maintaining consistent engineering standards. This is an important architectural and organizational consideration. AI adoption cannot scale sustainably through isolated experiments. It needs an engineering operating model. So, what does AI engineering really mean? I would describe AI engineering as the discipline of designing, building, integrating, deploying, and operating software systems that use AI capabilities to solve real-world problems reliably and responsibly. It brings together several established engineering disciplines: Software architecture and application engineering. Data engineering and context management. Machine learning and model integration. Distributed systems and orchestration. Platform engineering and infrastructure. Security, governance, and operational excellence. Quality engineering and continuous evaluation. It does not mean every software engineer needs to become a machine learning researcher. Nor does it mean every application needs autonomous agents, complex RAG pipelines, or multiple language models. Sometimes a traditional API, a well-designed database query, or a deterministic business rule is still the better solution. Good engineering is about choosing the right approach for the problem, not introducing AI simply because it is available. That judgment becomes even more important as AI capabilities continue to evolve. My perspective: The next engineering challenge is not building with AI. It is engineering around AI. I am genuinely excited about what AI is making possible in software engineering and enterprise technology. We are seeing new ways to interact with systems, automate complex workflows, improve developer productivity, and make organizational knowledge more accessible. But I also think we need to be careful about equating rapid experimentation with engineering maturity. A working prototype is a good beginning. A compelling demonstration is an encouraging milestone. Neither establishes that we have built something ready for enterprise adoption. The real test begins when the application encounters unpredictable inputs, incomplete information, security boundaries, integration failures, operational constraints, and real business expectations. That is where engineering discipline matters. We need architects who understand how AI capabilities fit into broader enterprise systems. We need engineers who understand both traditional software principles and the uncertainty introduced by language models. We need platform teams that can provide reusable foundations. And we need technology leaders who understand that successful AI adoption is as much about operating models, governance, and measurable outcomes as it is about technology. Prompt engineering helped us discover what AI can do. AI engineering will determine whether we can depend on it. And I believe that is where the next chapter of software engineering begins.

Some time ago, I watched an organization spend the better part of six months producing a target-state architecture for a modernization program. The document was impressive. Sixty-odd pages. Layered capability maps, integration views, a data architecture, a transition roadmap, and a beautifully colour-coded picture of how everything would look in three years. It was presented to the steering committee, praised, approved, and filed. Eighteen months later, I asked a delivery lead on one of the programs how the target state was influencing their work. They paused, then asked, "Which version?" That answer has stayed with me. Not because the architects did poor work. They were capable people who did exactly what they had been asked to do. But what they had been asked to produce was the wrong thing. To me, architecture is not the production of diagrams, standards, and review meetings. The real purpose of architecture is to improve the quality, speed, and durability of decisions. Everything else is a by-product. Start with the decision, not the drawing Consider two architects given the same problem. A business unit wants to launch a new customer onboarding journey. Customer data is spread across a CRM platform, a legacy policy system, and a handful of spreadsheets that nobody likes to talk about. The first architect starts drawing. Current state, target state, integration patterns, a canonical data model. Three weeks later there is a comprehensive pack. It is accurate. It is also too broad for anyone to act on, and the delivery team has already started building because the business deadline did not wait. The second architect starts with a question: what decision do we actually need to make, and by when? It turns out there are only three that matter in the next quarter: Where should the customer master record live? Do we integrate directly with the legacy system or put an API layer in front of it? What is the minimum data quality we need before launch? The architect writes a short decision record for each one. The options, the trade-offs, the recommendation, and the risks being accepted. Each is two pages at most. The diagrams that exist are there because they help explain a choice, not because a template required them. Both architects worked hard. Only one of them changed the outcome. I'd rather have a one-page decision record that people actually use than forty diagrams that people admire. Architecture that cannot be operated is not architecture One of the most expensive mistakes I've seen is a technically elegant design that the organization simply could not run. A team, enthusiastic about event-driven architecture, introduced a streaming platform to decouple a set of order-processing services. On paper, it was the right pattern. Loose coupling, independent scaling, a clean audit trail. In practice, nobody in the operations team had run that platform before. Monitoring was an afterthought. Consumer lag went unnoticed until customers started calling. When a partition issue surfaced on a Saturday night, the only person who understood the setup was on holiday. Within a year, the organization was paying for a specialist support contract and quietly routing the most important flows back through the old synchronous integration "for stability." The pattern was not wrong. The architecture was. Good architecture takes the operating reality into account from the start: the skills the teams actually have, the support model, security controls, funding cycles, and how much change the organization can absorb. A design that ignores those constraints isn't ambitious. It's incomplete. I believe an architect should be able to answer a simple question about any significant recommendation: who will run this at 2 a.m., and do they know how? Governance should create guardrails, not queues Most organizations eventually create an architecture review board. The intent is good: consistency, risk management, alignment with enterprise principles. But I've seen too many boards turn into queues. Teams prepare elaborate submissions. They wait two or three weeks for a slot. They receive a list of questions, revise, and return. The well-run teams experience it as a tax. The teams that most need guidance learn to present their designs in a way that passes the review, then build something slightly different. When that happens, the board isn't governing architecture. It is governing paperwork. The approach I find far more effective has three parts: A small number of non-negotiable rules. Security, data residency, identity, and a handful of integration standards. These are enforced, ideally through automation rather than meetings. Paved roads. Reference architectures, templates, and platform defaults that make the right way the easiest way. Decision records owned by the teams. Visible to everyone, reviewed by architects when the risk or cost justifies it, not by default. Within those boundaries, teams decide. Architects spend their time where the stakes are high, not reviewing the fifteenth variation of a standard web application. And if teams consistently route around the architecture function, I don't see that as a compliance problem. I see it as feedback. It usually means the function is offering less value than it is costing in time. Optimize for change, not for the picture The best architecture is rarely the one with the most components or the newest technology. It is the one that lets the organization respond to change without repeatedly rebuilding its foundations. A simple example illustrates this. I came across an environment where fourteen applications read from and wrote to the same shared database. It had started as a sensible shortcut years earlier. By the time anyone looked closely, a single column change required impact analysis across six teams, a coordinated release, and roughly three months of calendar time. Nobody had designed it to be that way. It had simply accumulated, one reasonable decision at a time. No target-state diagram would have fixed that. What fixed it, gradually, was a series of deliberate decisions: put an API in front of the most contested data, give each domain clear ownership of its records, and stop new applications from connecting directly. That is what optimizing for change looks like in practice. Deliberate boundaries, clear ownership, observable systems, and an honest understanding of coupling. It is rarely glamorous, and it rarely shows up well in a slide. But it is the difference between a technology estate that can evolve and one that has to be replaced. Measure architecture by what it improves If architecture is a business capability, it should be measured like one. Not by the number of documents produced or reviews completed, but by the decisions it improves and the friction it removes. The measures I find most useful are: How long does it take to make a significant technology decision, from question to commitment? Is lead time for change getting shorter in the areas where architecture has been involved? Are the same integration and data problems recurring, or are they being designed out? Is operational risk reducing, and is ownership becoming clearer? These are harder to report than artifact counts. They also tell you whether the function is actually working. My perspective: architects should own outcomes I have come to believe that the most important change an architecture function can make is to stay with its decisions after they are made. An architect who recommends an approach and then moves on before it reaches production has given advice. Valuable, perhaps. But architecture, as I see it, includes being accountable for whether the decision held up. Did the integration stabilize? Did the platform land within the operating cost we expected? Did the team become faster, or did we simply move complexity somewhere less visible? When architects carry that accountability, their recommendations change. They become more pragmatic. "It depends" starts arriving with an explanation of what it depends on . The relationship with delivery teams shifts from reviewer and reviewed to people solving the same problem. There are environments, particularly regulated ones, where artifacts genuinely matter. Auditors need evidence, and control mappings need to exist. I don't dismiss that. But I'd be careful not to let the audit format become the design process for everything else. My view is simple: architecture is a business capability, not a drawing practice. Its job is to help the organization make better technology decisions, make them faster, and make them executable. If it isn't doing that, more diagrams won't help. The best architecture isn't the one with the most impressive picture. It's the one the organization can still change, run, and trust three years later.

Delegation is one of the most frequently discussed management skills. Almost every leadership conversation emphasizes the importance of delegating work, empowering teams, and developing people. Yet, in practice, I have seen a significant difference between what managers believe delegation means and what effective delegation actually looks like. Some managers delegate by assigning tasks. They tell someone what needs to be done, provide a deadline, and expect the work to be completed. Others delegate by transferring ownership. They explain the desired outcome, provide the necessary context, clarify decision-making authority, establish expectations, and allow the individual to determine how to deliver. These two approaches might look similar initially. But their long-term impact on people and organizations is very different. Assigning work creates activity. Transferring ownership creates accountability. The familiar delegation problem Imagine a manager asking an engineering lead to take ownership of a platform modernization initiative. The manager says: "We need to upgrade the platform. Put together a plan, coordinate with the teams, track the progress, and make sure we finish by the end of the quarter." The engineering lead accepts the responsibility. A few days later, they discover that several application teams have competing priorities. Infrastructure resources are limited. Security requirements need clarification. There are architectural dependencies that require decisions from another group. The lead starts coordinating meetings and following up with stakeholders. But whenever a decision needs to be made, they return to the manager. The manager responds by making the decisions, negotiating with other teams, and providing further instructions. Eventually, the engineering lead becomes responsible for tracking and coordinating the initiative, while the manager retains actual ownership of the important decisions. This is a common delegation failure. The responsibility has been assigned, but the authority has not been transferred. The individual is accountable for an outcome they cannot fully control. That is not empowerment. Delegation requires more than assigning a task I believe effective delegation has five essential elements. 1. Clarity of outcomes People need to understand what success looks like. Instead of saying, "Improve our deployment process," explain the intended outcome. For example: "We want engineering teams to independently provision environments and deploy applications through standardized pipelines, reducing manual dependencies and improving deployment consistency." The second statement provides context and direction. It allows the person to evaluate different approaches instead of simply following instructions. 2. Authority to make decisions Responsibility without decision-making authority creates frustration. If someone owns a modernization initiative, they should have the authority to make appropriate technical and operational decisions within agreed boundaries. This doesn't mean every decision should be unrestricted. Architecture standards, security requirements, financial approvals, and enterprise policies still matter. But the boundaries should be explicit. People should know which decisions they can make independently, which require consultation, and which need formal approval. 3. Access to resources Delegation also requires enabling people with the resources needed to succeed. That includes engineering capacity, tools, information, stakeholder access, and organizational support. Assigning someone a critical initiative without addressing resource constraints is not delegation. It is setting them up for failure. 4. Accountability and measurable expectations Ownership should be accompanied by measurable outcomes. For a platform engineering initiative, these might include: Number of applications onboarded to standardized deployment patterns. Reduction in manual deployment activities. Adoption of self-service capabilities. Improvement in deployment frequency and reliability. Reduction in operational dependencies. The objective is to evaluate results, not continuously monitor every activity. 5. Support without interference This is where leadership judgment becomes important. The manager should remain available to coach, challenge, and remove obstacles. But support should not become constant interference. There is a difference between asking someone how they are progressing and telling them exactly how to execute every step. The former creates accountability. The latter can undermine ownership. The difference between a status update and an ownership conversation I also think managers should reconsider the way they conduct follow-ups. A typical status conversation often revolves around questions such as: What did you complete yesterday? What are you working on today? Why is this taking longer? Have you followed up with everyone? When will this be completed? These questions are not necessarily wrong. Operational visibility matters. But if every conversation focuses on individual activities, managers can unintentionally create a culture where people optimize for reporting work rather than owning outcomes. An ownership-oriented conversation is different. It asks: Are we on track to achieve the intended outcome? What risks could prevent us from succeeding? What decisions do you need to make? Which dependencies are outside your control? What support do you need from me? What would you change if you were responsible for this initiative end to end? The difference is subtle but meaningful. The manager is still engaged, but the individual is expected to think, evaluate, and lead. Delegation also means allowing people to make mistakes This is perhaps the hardest part for many managers. We often delegate work but struggle to accept that someone might approach it differently from how we would. When an individual makes a decision that doesn't produce the expected outcome, the immediate reaction can be to step in, take control, and prevent further mistakes. Sometimes that intervention is necessary. But if every mistake results in the manager taking back ownership, people quickly learn not to make independent decisions. They become cautious. They seek approval for everything. They avoid responsibility because the cost of getting something wrong is too high. I believe managers need to distinguish between mistakes caused by negligence and mistakes that happen as part of learning and exercising judgment. A technical decision that doesn't work as expected can become a valuable learning opportunity. The important questions are whether the decision was made responsibly, whether the risks were understood, whether appropriate guardrails existed, and whether the individual learned from the outcome. If we expect people to develop judgment, we must give them opportunities to exercise it. Delegation changes as people grow Not everyone needs the same level of delegation. A new engineer might need detailed guidance, frequent feedback, and clearly defined tasks. An experienced technical lead should be able to own a technical workstream and coordinate dependencies independently. An engineering manager should be capable of managing delivery, people, and stakeholder expectations. A senior leader should be able to translate business objectives into organizational priorities and develop the next level of leadership. The degree of direction should evolve with the individual's experience, capability, and the complexity of the work. Treating an experienced leader like a junior team member is counterproductive. Equally, giving someone a broad responsibility without the necessary preparation or support is not empowerment. Good delegation requires judgment. The manager needs to understand the individual's strengths, identify development opportunities, and gradually expand their decision-making responsibilities. My perspective: Delegate ownership, not just workload I don't see delegation as a way for managers to reduce their own workload. That may be a benefit, but it shouldn't be the primary objective. The real value of delegation is organizational capability development. When I delegate something, I should be thinking about more than who can complete the task. I should be thinking about who can grow by owning it. Can this person lead a cross-functional discussion? Can they make a difficult technical decision? Can they manage stakeholder expectations? Can they develop a solution rather than wait for instructions? These are opportunities to develop future leaders. I also believe managers should be comfortable with the fact that delegated work may not be completed exactly the way they would have done it. If the outcome meets expectations, the decisions are sound, and the approach respects organizational guardrails, different approaches should be welcomed. The objective isn't to create a team of people who think exactly like the manager. It is to create a team of people who can think independently and deliver collectively. Ultimately, delegation should follow a simple principle: Give people the responsibility, authority, context, and resources to own an outcome. Stay available to support them, but resist the temptation to take control back at the first sign of difficulty. If you delegate tasks, you get people who execute. If you delegate ownership, you develop people who lead. The purpose of delegation isn't to distribute your workload. It is to multiply the number of people capable of delivering meaningful outcomes.

There is a subtle difference between being involved as a leader and being involved in everything. I've seen managers who know every task their team members are working on, every email being sent, every conversation happening, and every decision being considered. They attend every meeting, review every deliverable, question every deviation, and expect to be copied on practically everything. At first glance, this might look like strong leadership. There is visibility, involvement, and a sense of control. But I often wonder: If everything needs your attention, what exactly have you enabled your team to do independently? To me, leadership is not about becoming the central point through which every decision, activity, and outcome must pass. It is about building a team that has the clarity, confidence, capability, and authority to move forward without constantly looking over its shoulder. The difference between managing work and enabling people Consider two different situations. A critical production issue surfaces. A team of engineers is investigating the problem. In the first situation, the manager immediately takes charge. They ask for updates every 15 minutes, dictate which engineer should investigate which component, question every technical decision, and insist that all proposed changes come to them for approval. The team eventually resolves the issue. The manager feels accomplished because they were involved throughout the process. But what happens the next time a similar issue occurs? The team waits for the manager again. Nobody wants to make a decision independently because they have learned that decisions belong to the manager. Now consider a different approach. The manager establishes the severity of the issue, clarifies the expected outcome, ensures the team has access to the necessary resources, and identifies any organizational dependencies that need escalation. The engineers take ownership of the investigation. They collaborate, evaluate alternatives, make technical decisions within agreed boundaries, and communicate progress. The manager remains available, removes obstacles, challenges assumptions when necessary, and steps in when the situation requires leadership intervention. The outcome might be exactly the same: the production issue gets resolved. But the long-term impact is very different. In the first situation, the organization has resolved an incident with the manager's involvement. In the second, it has developed a team that is better equipped to resolve the next incident independently. One approach solves today's problem. The other builds tomorrow's capability. That distinction matters. Micromanagement creates dependency, not accountability One of the biggest misconceptions in management is that more oversight automatically translates into better accountability. It doesn't. When people are constantly instructed on what to do, how to do it, when to do it, and whom to consult, they gradually stop exercising independent judgment. They become comfortable executing instructions rather than owning outcomes. Over time, a predictable pattern emerges: People escalate decisions they are perfectly capable of making. Managers become bottlenecks for routine activities. Teams optimize for keeping the manager informed rather than delivering meaningful outcomes. Employees avoid taking risks because independent decisions might attract criticism. Managers become increasingly overwhelmed because everything depends on them. Ironically, the manager who believes they are improving accountability may actually be weakening it. I believe accountability should come with ownership. If I expect someone to be accountable for an outcome, I must also give them the authority, context, and resources to influence that outcome. Holding someone responsible for results while retaining control over every decision is not empowerment. It is an organizational contradiction. Leadership means creating clarity, not providing constant instructions Imagine assigning a team the responsibility of improving vulnerability remediation across an enterprise technology environment. A micromanaging approach might involve daily instructions about which vulnerabilities to address, who should work on them, what sequence to follow, and how every remediation activity should be executed. An enabling leader would approach the problem differently. They would establish the business objective, define risk-based priorities, agree on remediation timelines and service-level expectations, make ownership explicit, and ensure the team has the necessary tools and support. For example, the leader might establish a clear expectation that critical vulnerabilities must be addressed within defined timelines and that supported technology versions must remain within an agreed upgrade threshold. The team then determines how best to achieve those objectives. They identify dependencies, coordinate with application owners, plan remediation waves, automate repetitive activities, and proactively escalate blockers. The leader reviews outcomes, challenges delays, questions ineffective approaches, and helps resolve issues beyond the team's authority. Notice what has changed. The leader hasn't reduced accountability or lowered expectations. They have simply shifted their attention from controlling activities to enabling outcomes. Clear expectations create direction. Autonomy creates ownership. Accountability ensures results. All three are necessary. Being available is not the same as being involved in everything I strongly believe leaders should remain accessible to their teams. People should feel comfortable approaching their managers with challenges, disagreements, ideas, and difficult decisions. However, accessibility should not become dependency. There is a difference between a team member seeking guidance and a team member seeking permission for every action. For example, if an architect approaches me with two possible technology solutions, I would rather understand their evaluation, trade-offs, recommendation, and reasoning than immediately prescribe which solution they should implement. I might challenge their assumptions. I might ask questions they haven't considered. I might disagree with their recommendation. But the objective should be to improve their thinking and decision-making capability, not demonstrate that I know more than they do. Sometimes, the best thing a leader can do is ask one more question instead of providing one more instruction. This is particularly important when building the next generation of technical and organizational leaders. If every difficult decision continues to come back to the same manager, the organization hasn't developed leadership capacity. It has simply created a dependency on one individual. Trust doesn't mean the absence of governance There is another misconception worth addressing. Empowering teams doesn't mean allowing everyone to operate independently without structure, standards, or oversight. That would be a recipe for inconsistency. In technology organizations, architecture standards, security controls, operational governance, financial discipline, and engineering practices are essential. The question is not whether governance should exist. The question is how it should work. For instance, an architecture review board should establish guardrails, ensure alignment with enterprise principles, identify risks, and challenge design decisions. It should not become a mechanism where every engineering decision requires a committee's approval. Similarly, engineering standards should guide teams toward consistency without eliminating their ability to innovate. I see leadership as establishing the boundaries within which teams can operate confidently. Within those boundaries, teams should have the freedom to make decisions, experiment, learn, and improve. Trust and governance are not opposites. Good governance makes responsible autonomy possible. A leader's success is measured by what happens in their absence Here is a question I believe every manager should occasionally ask themselves: If I were unavailable for the next two weeks, would my team continue to operate effectively? Not whether they would survive two weeks by simply waiting for me to return. Would they continue making decisions? Would they resolve problems? Would they manage stakeholders? Would they maintain operational commitments? Would they know when and how to escalate something genuinely requiring leadership intervention? If the answer is no, there is an opportunity to rethink how the team is being led. Perhaps responsibilities are unclear. Perhaps decision-making authority has never been delegated. Perhaps people have not been given enough opportunities to develop their judgment. Or perhaps the manager has unintentionally made themselves indispensable. I don't consider being indispensable a leadership achievement. I consider creating an organization that can perform, adapt, and grow without depending on one individual a much greater achievement. This also changes how I think about delegation. Delegation isn't simply distributing tasks to reduce a manager's workload. It is transferring ownership, developing judgment, and creating opportunities for people to grow. A leader should deliberately create space for others to lead. That means allowing people to make decisions, occasionally make mistakes, learn from those mistakes, and become better at what they do. Of course, the leader remains accountable for the environment, the guardrails, and the overall direction. Empowerment is not an excuse to walk away from responsibility. It is a commitment to develop responsibility in others. My perspective: Leadership is about multiplying capability I have come to believe that leadership effectiveness should not be measured by how many decisions a manager makes, how many meetings they attend, or how many activities they personally oversee. It should be measured by how much capability they create around them. A good leader should make their team stronger, not more dependent. They should make decision-making faster, not centralize it. They should create confidence, not fear of making mistakes. They should develop people who can challenge ideas, take ownership, and eventually lead others. And perhaps most importantly, they should recognize that their role changes as the organization matures. Early in a team's development, people may need more direction, structure, and hands-on guidance. As their experience and confidence grow, the leader must consciously step back and create room for greater ownership. Continuing to operate with the same level of control regardless of the team's maturity is not effective leadership. It is an inability to evolve as a leader. I would rather have a team that challenges my thinking, makes informed decisions, takes accountability, and occasionally disagrees with me than a team that agrees with everything I say and waits for my next instruction. Because ultimately, leadership isn't about having the smartest person in the room make every decision. It is about creating a room full of capable people who can make great decisions together. My definition of leadership is simple: Give people direction, provide them with the tools and context to succeed, establish the boundaries within which they can operate, trust them to deliver, and stand behind them when they need support. Don't build a team that needs you for everything. Build a team that becomes better because of you. Leadership is not about being the person everyone waits for. It is about building an environment where people have the confidence and capability to move forward without waiting.

There is something interesting about managers who always seem to be in the middle of every problem. A production issue occurs, and they are the first to jump in. A project gets delayed, and they immediately take over. A stakeholder raises a concern, and they personally start coordinating the resolution. A team member struggles with a decision, and they step in to make it. They are always available, always involved, and seemingly always busy. From the outside, these managers often look like dedicated leaders who go above and beyond for their teams. But I think there is a question worth asking: Are they actually building a stronger organization, or are they building an organization that cannot function without them? I call this the hero syndrome in leadership. It is the tendency of managers to position themselves as the person who can solve every problem, make every important decision, and rescue every difficult situation. Initially, this behavior might even be rewarded. Stakeholders appreciate the quick response. Senior leadership sees someone taking ownership. Teams appreciate having someone who can step in when things get difficult. But over time, the same behavior can become one of the biggest organizational bottlenecks. The manager who always saves the day Consider a familiar situation in a technology organization. A critical delivery milestone is at risk. There are dependencies across engineering, infrastructure, security, and business teams. The manager recognizes the urgency and immediately gets involved. They start coordinating meetings, following up with individual contributors, negotiating timelines, making technical decisions, and communicating updates to senior stakeholders. Eventually, the milestone is delivered. Everyone appreciates the manager's contribution. But something important has happened along the way. The engineers have not learned how to independently manage cross-functional dependencies. The technical leads have not developed the confidence to drive difficult conversations. The next-level managers have not had the opportunity to demonstrate ownership. The manager has solved the immediate problem, but the organization has not necessarily become better at solving similar problems. The next time a comparable situation occurs, everyone looks to the same manager. And the cycle repeats. The manager becomes busier, the team becomes increasingly dependent, and the organization starts treating individual heroics as a normal operating model. When the same person has to repeatedly rescue the organization, perhaps the problem isn't the absence of a hero. Perhaps the problem is the operating model. Why managers fall into the hero trap I don't necessarily believe managers consciously set out to create dependency. In many cases, the behavior comes from good intentions. They want things done correctly. They don't want their teams to fail. They feel accountable for outcomes and believe that stepping in is the fastest way to get things moving. There are also organizational incentives that reinforce this behavior. A manager who personally resolves a critical issue is visible. A manager who quietly develops three capable leaders might receive much less recognition. Immediate results are easier to demonstrate than long-term capability building. But there is a difference between taking ownership and taking over. Taking ownership means ensuring the problem gets resolved, even when the actual work is performed by someone else. Taking over means assuming responsibility for activities and decisions that should belong to the team. The first is leadership. The second can become dependency. The hidden cost of being indispensable The hero syndrome has consequences that are not always immediately visible. 1. It creates a decision-making bottleneck When every important decision needs managerial intervention, execution slows down. People stop evaluating alternatives independently because they expect the manager to make the final call. Even experienced architects and engineering managers may hesitate to move forward without approval. 2. It limits the development of future leaders People develop leadership capability by being given opportunities to lead. If the manager always takes over difficult conversations, stakeholder escalations, and critical decisions, the next generation of leaders never gets enough exposure. They remain good executors but struggle to become independent leaders. 3. It creates an unsustainable workload The manager becomes the escalation point for everything. Routine decisions, operational issues, project dependencies, and stakeholder conversations all compete for the same person's attention. Eventually, strategic thinking gets displaced by operational firefighting. 4. It creates a false sense of organizational strength The organization may appear to be performing well because one individual is compensating for weaknesses across the system. But what happens when that person is unavailable, changes roles, or leaves? The dependency becomes visible very quickly. An organization should not confuse the effectiveness of an individual hero with the maturity of its operating model. The difference between stepping in and taking over I don't believe leaders should stay away from problems just to demonstrate that they are delegating. There are situations where direct intervention is necessary. A major security incident, a business-critical outage, a serious compliance concern, or a decision with significant enterprise-wide consequences may require immediate leadership involvement. The distinction is in what happens after the immediate situation is under control. For example, consider a recurring vulnerability remediation problem. A manager could personally coordinate every application owner, chase every remediation commitment, and escalate every delay. That might improve short-term visibility. But an enabling leader would look at the underlying system. Are ownership responsibilities clear? Are remediation timelines defined? Are dependencies tracked? Do application teams have the resources to upgrade? Are recurring blockers being addressed? Is there sufficient automation? The leader should establish accountability, remove organizational barriers, and ensure the right operating mechanisms exist. The team should own execution. The objective is not to make the manager less accountable. It is to make the organization less dependent on the manager's personal intervention. Your real job is to develop people who can replace you This is perhaps the most important shift in mindset. As managers, we should actively create opportunities for others to take ownership of responsibilities that we previously handled ourselves. Let a technical lead run the architecture discussion. Let an engineering manager handle a difficult stakeholder conversation. Let a senior engineer lead a production incident review. Let someone else present the team's progress to senior leadership. They may not handle everything exactly the way you would. They may make mistakes. They may need guidance. They may take longer initially. That is part of developing capability. The manager's role is to provide context, set expectations, establish boundaries, coach, and intervene when necessary. It is not to ensure that everyone performs tasks in exactly the same way the manager would. If you never give people the opportunity to operate independently, you cannot expect them to become independent. My perspective: Stop celebrating organizational dependency I have come to believe that being indispensable is often an overrated measure of leadership success. A manager who personally resolves every difficult situation may be a very capable individual contributor, but that alone does not make them an effective organizational leader. Leadership is about multiplying capability. It is about creating systems, developing people, establishing accountability, and building an environment where good decisions can happen at every level. I would rather see an organization where five leaders can independently manage their respective areas than one manager who personally controls all five. I would rather see a team that can resolve problems without waiting for managerial instructions than one that consistently depends on a manager to rescue it. And I would rather spend time developing the next generation of leaders than constantly proving that I can solve every problem myself. There is a simple test I would encourage every manager to consider: If your absence creates confusion, delays, and uncertainty across the organization, you may have built dependency instead of leadership capability. Your success should not be measured by how many problems require your intervention. It should be measured by how many problems your team can solve because of the capability you helped them develop. Don't aim to be the hero everyone depends on. Aim to be the leader who makes heroes unnecessary. The strongest leaders don't build organizations around themselves. They build organizations that are strong enough to succeed without them.

One of the most concerning things I have observed in organizations is not a lack of technical skills or experience. It is the gradual disappearance of independent thinking. You attend a meeting and ask for recommendations. Nobody offers one. You ask a technical lead how they would approach a problem. They respond by asking what you would prefer. You assign an initiative and expect the person responsible to come back with a plan. Instead, they return with a list of questions about what they should do next. At some point, you begin to wonder whether the team has the necessary capability to operate independently. But I think there is another possibility worth considering. What if the organization has gradually trained people not to think for themselves? It doesn't happen overnight. It develops through repeated interactions, management practices, and organizational behaviors that unintentionally discourage initiative. How independent thinking disappears Consider a technical design discussion. An architect presents a proposed solution. The manager immediately questions the approach, suggests an alternative, and directs the architect to revise the design. The architect goes back and makes the changes. A few weeks later, another design is presented. The same thing happens. Eventually, the architect stops putting forward a recommendation. Instead, they ask the manager what approach they should take before investing time in developing a solution. From the manager's perspective, the architect may appear to lack initiative. But from the architect's perspective, there is little incentive to exercise independent judgment when the manager consistently overrides it. The behavior is learned. People begin to understand what is expected of them. They stop preparing recommendations and start preparing options for someone else to decide. They stop challenging assumptions and start seeking agreement. They stop owning outcomes and start following instructions. This is how excessive control gradually weakens independent thinking. The approval culture Another common symptom is an organization where almost everything requires approval. A technical lead cannot finalize a design without managerial sign-off. An engineering manager cannot adjust priorities without seeking permission. A team member cannot communicate a delivery risk to a stakeholder without first consulting their manager. Even routine operational decisions become escalation points. Of course, some decisions should require approval. Financial commitments, significant architectural changes, security exceptions, and business-critical risks may need formal governance. But when the approval process extends to routine decisions, it creates unnecessary dependency. It also sends a message. The message is that independent judgment is not trusted. Over time, people adapt. Why take responsibility for a decision when someone else can make it? Why risk disagreement when approval is safer? Why think through alternatives when the manager will eventually prescribe the answer? The organization ends up with a culture of compliance rather than ownership. The difference between asking questions and challenging thinking I believe managers play an important role in developing independent thinking. But this requires changing how we interact with people. Imagine an engineer approaching you with a technical problem. One response is to immediately provide the solution. You know the technology, understand the architecture, and have probably encountered something similar before. Providing the answer is quick. But consider a different response. Ask the engineer: What do you believe is causing the problem? What alternatives have you considered? What are the trade-offs? Which approach would you recommend? What risks do you see? What would you do if I weren't available? The conversation becomes an opportunity to develop reasoning. You can challenge assumptions, introduce considerations they may have missed, and help them evaluate alternatives. But the individual still owns the thinking. I don't believe a manager needs to have the answer to every question. Sometimes, asking the right question is far more valuable than providing an immediate solution. This is particularly important in technology leadership, where problems are rarely identical and solutions require context-specific judgment. We should be developing people who can reason through unfamiliar situations, not simply reproduce solutions from previous experiences. Psychological safety and the fear of being wrong There is another important dimension to this problem. People will not exercise independent judgment if they believe every mistake will be treated as a failure. Think about an engineering team working on a modernization initiative. One engineer proposes an alternative architecture. The proposal is challenged aggressively in a meeting. The engineer is criticized for not considering every possible dependency. The discussion ends with the manager prescribing the solution. What does the rest of the team learn? Probably not that they should bring better proposals next time. They learn that proposing something different can be risky. They begin to keep their ideas to themselves. This is why I believe psychological safety matters in leadership. It doesn't mean lowering standards or avoiding difficult conversations. It means creating an environment where people can disagree respectfully, raise concerns, challenge decisions, and admit uncertainty without fear of humiliation. A team should be able to say: "I disagree with this approach, and here is why." It should also be able to say: "I made the wrong decision. Here is what happened, and here is what I learned." Leaders need to distinguish between an honest mistake made through responsible decision-making and careless behavior that disregards established expectations. If we want people to think independently, we must make it safe for them to express independent thinking. When agreement becomes more important than good decisions I have always believed that a team where everyone agrees with the manager is not necessarily a healthy team. In fact, it can be a warning sign. Consider an architecture review where everyone accepts the proposed solution without questioning its scalability, security implications, operational complexity, or long-term cost. The meeting finishes quickly. But has the organization made a good decision? Perhaps not. Healthy technical organizations need constructive disagreement. Architects should challenge engineering decisions. Engineers should question architectural assumptions. Security teams should identify risks. Operations teams should challenge designs that create unnecessary operational complexity. The objective isn't to win arguments. It is to make better decisions. A leader should welcome a well-reasoned disagreement, even when it challenges their own recommendation. If people learn that agreement is rewarded more consistently than critical thinking, they will eventually optimize for agreement. And the organization will lose one of its most valuable capabilities: the ability to challenge itself. Autonomy needs guardrails, not constant supervision There is an important distinction between giving people autonomy and allowing everyone to operate without alignment. Independent thinking does not mean independent direction. Teams need shared objectives, architectural principles, security standards, financial boundaries, and clear accountability. For example, an engineering organization can establish enterprise architecture standards and security requirements while allowing individual teams to determine how best to implement solutions within those boundaries. Similarly, a platform engineering organization can provide golden paths, standardized deployment pipelines, and reusable capabilities without dictating every engineering decision. The purpose of guardrails is to make responsible decision-making easier. They should not become another mechanism for centralizing control. Good leadership creates clarity about what cannot be compromised while allowing flexibility in how outcomes are achieved. Rebuilding a culture of independent thinking If a team has become accustomed to seeking instructions, changing that behavior requires patience and consistency. Managers cannot spend years centralizing decisions and suddenly expect everyone to become autonomous. It requires deliberate effort. A few practices can make a meaningful difference. Ask for recommendations, not just updates. Instead of asking what someone has completed, ask what they recommend doing next and why. Give people ownership of decisions. Start with decisions that have manageable risks and gradually expand their authority. Encourage constructive disagreement. Make it clear that challenging an idea is not the same as challenging someone's authority. Avoid immediately providing answers.
