Give people time to think, evaluate, and propose solutions before stepping in. Recognize good judgment, not just successful outcomes. A well-reasoned decision can still produce an unexpected result. Recognize the quality of the thinking, not only whether the outcome was perfect. Be consistent. If managers encourage independent thinking but repeatedly override decisions without explanation, the culture will not change. The behavior of leadership must match the expectations being placed on the team. My perspective: Don't create followers when you need thinkers I believe one of the biggest responsibilities of leadership is to develop people who can think beyond the instructions they receive. A team that executes instructions efficiently has value. But a team that can identify problems, challenge assumptions, evaluate alternatives, make decisions, and take ownership creates much greater organizational capability. This becomes even more important as technology organizations evolve. With automation and AI increasingly taking over routine execution, the value of human judgment, problem-solving, critical thinking, and decision-making becomes even more important. We should be building teams that can think, not simply teams that can execute. I would rather have an engineer who challenges my technical recommendation with sound reasoning than one who agrees with everything I say. I would rather have an architect who identifies a weakness in an enterprise design than one who simply implements it without question. And I would rather have an engineering manager who independently resolves difficult situations than one who constantly escalates decisions that should be theirs to make. As leaders, we should periodically ask ourselves: Are we developing people who can make better decisions, or are we developing people who are simply getting better at asking us for decisions? There is a significant difference. If your team has stopped thinking independently, don't start by demanding more initiative. First, examine whether your leadership practices actually encourage it. Because people don't develop ownership simply because it appears in their job description. They develop it when they are trusted, given opportunities, supported through challenges, and held accountable for meaningful outcomes. The goal of leadership is not to create a team that follows instructions perfectly. It is to create a team that understands the purpose, thinks critically, makes sound decisions, and takes responsibility for the results. Don't measure your team's effectiveness by how well they follow your instructions. Measure it by how well they think and perform when you aren't giving any. If every decision requires your opinion, you may have built a team that knows how to follow you but has never learned how to lead itself.

I have yet to see an AI demo fail in a steering committee. The pattern is familiar. Someone builds an internal knowledge assistant over a weekend. It is connected to a few hundred policy documents and a capable model. In the meeting, it answers ten questions fluently, cites its sources, and even handles a follow-up with a little humour. The room is impressed. Funding is approved. A pilot is launched with a few hundred users. Three weeks later, the first serious complaint arrives. An employee asked about the leave policy and received a confident, well-written, and completely outdated answer. The assistant had retrieved a document from two years ago that nobody had removed from the index. Nothing about the demo was dishonest. But it was curated. The presenter knew which questions worked, which documents were in the index, and which phrasing the model handled well. Real users know none of that. A demo shows that something is possible. It says very little about whether it is reliable. To me, that gap between "it worked in the demo" and "it works on Monday morning for four thousand people" is where AI engineering actually begins. Two teams, the same problem Consider two teams building the same capability: an assistant that helps service-desk agents resolve tickets faster. The first team iterates on prompts. Every time a user reports a bad answer, they adjust the instructions, try a few examples, and ship the change when it looks better. Reviews are lively but subjective. One person thinks the latest version is better; another has found a case where it is worse. When the model provider releases a new version, the behaviour shifts in ways nobody can quite explain. The second team does something less exciting first. They pull three hundred real tickets from the last six months, covering the common cases, the awkward ones, and a few that should be refused. With a couple of senior agents, they agree on what a good answer looks like for each. Then they automate the comparison, so every change to the prompt, the model, the retrieval logic, or the documents is scored against that set before it reaches users. For the first month, the second team looks slower. By the third month, they are the only ones who can answer a simple question with confidence: is the system getting better or worse? That is why, before anything else, the first thing I ask any AI team is to show me their evaluation set. Not five hand-picked examples. A representative set, with a definition of "good" that someone other than the builder agreed to. Teams that have one ship with confidence. Teams that don't end up debating impressions in every review meeting. Treat the model as a dependency, not a colleague Conventional software dependencies behave consistently. A given input to a library produces the same output today and tomorrow. Language models do not work that way. Their behaviour is probabilistic. It changes across versions, sometimes subtly. They can fail confidently, in ways that look exactly like success. I believe that changes how we should design around them. Every model call deserves an explicit boundary. What are we asking the model to do? How do we validate what comes back? What does the product do when the answer is uncertain, malformed, or unavailable because the provider is having a bad day? A simple example: an assistant that drafts customer emails should never send them directly. It drafts; a person or a rules engine approves. The difference in design effort is small. The difference in risk is enormous. Keep deterministic things deterministic One of the most important design decisions in an AI system is deciding what the model should not do. I've seen a proposal for an agent that would handle customer refund requests end to end: read the complaint, check the order, decide on the refund, and issue it. It worked well in testing. It also meant that the refund policy, including the financial limits, effectively lived inside a prompt. "The model usually gets it right" is not a control. The better design used the model for what it does well: understanding the complaint, summarizing the history, and drafting a recommended action. The decision itself, including thresholds, eligibility rules, and approval limits, stayed in ordinary code that could be tested, audited, and explained. My rule of thumb is straightforward. Use language models where interpretation, synthesis, and flexible interaction create value. Keep authorization, financial calculations, safety limits, and compliance rules in deterministic systems where predictable behaviour is essential. Most "agents" should start as workflows Agentic systems are genuinely powerful, and I don't want to dismiss them. But I've noticed that many proposed agents are, on closer inspection, workflows with a model in the middle. If you can draw the steps on a whiteboard (retrieve the customer record, classify the request, draft a response, route for approval), then write those steps as code, and use the model only for the parts that genuinely need judgment. That approach is easier to test, easier to bound in cost, and much easier to explain when something goes wrong. Autonomy can be introduced gradually, in the specific places where evaluation shows the model makes better decisions than the fixed path. Earn the autonomy. Don't assume it. The operating model is the product Production AI needs the same discipline as any other critical system, and a few additional ones. Cost. A pilot with two hundred users can look inexpensive. The same design at twenty thousand users, with long conversations and large retrieved contexts, can cost an order of magnitude more than anyone budgeted. I've seen projects stall not because the technology failed, but because nobody modelled the cost per successful task before scaling. Security. Retrieval-based systems read documents, and documents can contain instructions. A malicious or simply careless piece of text in an indexed file can influence the model's behaviour. Access control must apply to what the assistant can retrieve, not just to who can open the chat window. Observability. Latency and token usage are easy to measure. The more meaningful signals are task success rate, how often a human has to correct the output, groundedness where it matters, and how the system behaves when it doesn't know. A product that says "I'm not sure, here's who can help" will earn more trust than one that is confidently wrong three percent of the time. Ownership. Someone needs to own the evaluation set, the index, the prompts, and the incident process. When an AI system gives a bad answer, "the model did it" is not an acceptable root cause. My perspective: evaluation is the specification I have come to believe that for AI systems, the evaluation set is the specification. In traditional software, we write requirements and test against them. In AI systems, the requirements are often too nuanced to write down precisely, but they can be demonstrated through examples: this question should get this kind of answer, this request should be refused, this ambiguity should trigger a clarifying question. Teams that invest in that early make better decisions about everything else, including which model to use, whether a change is an improvement, and when the system is ready for more users. There is a fair counterpoint. In early exploration, speed matters more than rigour, and building a full evaluation harness for an idea that may be abandoned next week is wasteful. I agree. The problem isn't skipping evaluation while exploring. The problem is shipping the exploration and calling it a product. My view: the transition from demo to product is not primarily a prompt-engineering exercise. It is an engineering and operating-model challenge, and the teams that treat it that way are the ones whose systems are still trusted a year later. A demo earns attention. Evaluation, guardrails, and operational discipline earn trust.

Most engineering leaders I know were promoted for being exceptionally good at solving problems. They were the engineer who could find the root cause when nobody else could. The one who understood how the systems really fit together. The one people called when something went badly wrong. Then they were given a team. Then a larger one. Then several teams. And many of them, quite naturally, kept doing what had made them successful: solving the hardest problems personally. I recognize that instinct because I've had it myself. When something difficult surfaces, stepping in feels like the responsible thing to do. It's faster. It's satisfying. The team is grateful. But somewhere along the way, I realized that the skill that gets you into leadership is often the one that limits you once you're there. A leader's real impact isn't how many problems they can solve. It's how many people they've developed who can solve problems without them. The hero pattern Consider a situation I've seen play out more than once. An engineering manager leads a group of around forty engineers across several teams. They are technically outstanding. They still review the most important pull requests, join every serious incident bridge, and are the final word on most design decisions. For a while, this works. Quality is high. Incidents are resolved quickly. Senior stakeholders trust the manager because, whenever something goes wrong, they're already on it. Then the cracks begin to show. Decisions queue up whenever the manager is in back-to-back meetings. Tech leads stop proposing designs and start asking what the manager would prefer. The strongest engineers, the ones with leadership potential, begin to leave, because there's no room for them to grow. And the manager is working sixty-hour weeks and still feels behind. Nobody intended this. The team didn't become dependent because they lacked ability. They became dependent because, every time a hard problem appeared, they learned that the real decision-maker would step in. Every rescue teaches the team something. Usually, it teaches them to wait. I wrote separately about why leadership is about enabling people rather than micromanaging them. Here I want to focus on what a leader should do instead: how to deliberately build capability that multiplies. Look at where your time actually goes One of the most useful exercises I know is uncomfortable but simple: look honestly at your calendar for the last four weeks. When I've done this, and when I've asked other leaders to do it, the result is usually surprising. A large share of time goes to status meetings, approvals, and problem-solving that someone else on the team could have handled. A small share goes to the things only a leader can do: setting direction, developing people, managing important relationships, and making the genuinely difficult trade-offs. A leader I once worked with found that nearly two-thirds of their week was spent in meetings whose primary purpose was to keep them informed. The team was effectively spending hours each week preparing updates for one person. They made a few changes. A weekly ninety-minute status meeting became a short written update that took five minutes to read. A focused thirty-minute risk review replaced several ad hoc check-ins. Routine approvals were delegated to tech leads with clear criteria. They didn't lose visibility. They gained something like a day a week, and they spent it on coaching and on the cross-team problems that had been waiting for months. Your calendar is the most honest statement of your leadership priorities. Delegate decisions, not just tasks There is a difference between giving someone work and giving them ownership. Handing out tasks while keeping every meaningful decision isn't really delegation. It's dispatch. The person does the work, but the judgment, and therefore the growth, stays with the leader. Real delegation means giving someone a decision area. For example: "You own the reliability of the payments platform. Here are the constraints: budget, compliance requirements, and the availability target we've committed to. Here's how we'll know it's working. Come to me when you need help or when something crosses these boundaries." Then comes the hard part: living with their decisions. Early on, those decisions may not be the ones you would have made. Some will be slower. Some will be worse. I've learned to accept that, within reason, because the alternative is worse. A good-enough decision made without me is often more valuable than a perfect one that depends on me. Only one of them scales. What I watch closely is not whether every decision matches mine, but whether the person's judgment is improving, and whether they know when to escalate. Build leaders, not just teams The leaders I admire most measure themselves partly by the leaders they leave behind. That doesn't happen by accident. It requires deliberately creating opportunities for others to lead, before they feel completely ready. Some of the most effective ways I've seen: Let a tech lead run quarterly planning for their area, with the leader as a reviewer rather than the author. Rotate incident command so that more than one person learns to lead under pressure. Send someone else to the steering committee to present their team's work, and support them rather than speak for them. Name potential successors explicitly and give them stretch responsibilities with real stakes. Each of these carries some risk. The planning might be rougher. The presentation might not land as well. But each one builds judgment and confidence in a way that watching never will. If no one on your team could step into your role within a year, that is worth reflecting on. It's a risk for the organization, and it usually means people aren't getting the opportunities they need to grow. Build a management system, not a dependency Strong teams don't rely on a leader's memory and attention to stay on track. They rely on a reliable operating rhythm. The systems I've found most effective are surprisingly simple: A small set of meaningful measures , such as delivery flow, reliability, and quality, reviewed regularly and trusted by everyone. A regular risk review , where problems are raised early, before they become escalations. Explicit commitments , written down, so that progress is visible without anyone needing to ask. A decision log , so that context survives beyond the meeting where a choice was made. The aim is to make work visible before it becomes a crisis. And one caution: status reporting can quietly become a substitute for progress. If teams spend more time describing their work than doing it, the system needs simplifying. My perspective: measure yourself by what happens without you I have come to believe that the most honest test of a leader is what happens when they're not there. Take a real holiday. Two weeks, genuinely offline. Then come back and look carefully. What broke? What waited for you? Which decisions didn't get made? Who stepped up? That list is your leadership backlog. It is a far better measure of effectiveness than how many fires you personally put out last quarter. There are times when a leader needs to be hands-on. During a major incident, a turnaround, or when a team has lost confidence, strong direct involvement can be exactly what's needed. I don't think stepping in is wrong. The risk is that crisis mode is comfortable for people like us, and "for a while" quietly becomes the way we operate. My view: the multiplier isn't how much a leader can do personally. It's how much keeps happening, and keeps happening well, after they step out of the room. Great engineers solve hard problems. Great engineering leaders build teams that solve the next ones without them.

I once sat through an annual technology strategy offsite that ended with fourteen strategic priorities. Every one of them was reasonable. Cloud adoption. Data platform modernization. API enablement. Zero trust security. Developer experience. Automation. AI. Observability. Customer 360. And several more. Each priority had an owner, a slide, and a target date. The final presentation looked comprehensive and confident. A year later, I looked at what had actually changed. The organization now had three integration platforms instead of two. Two migrations were roughly half complete, which meant both the old and new environments had to be funded and supported. Teams were stretched across so many initiatives that the most important ones had moved slowest of all. Nobody had made a bad decision. The problem was that nobody had made the hard ones. To me, a strategy that only says yes isn't a strategy. It's a wish list with a timeline. A roadmap is not a strategy Technology strategy is often presented as a roadmap: platforms to adopt, systems to migrate, capabilities to build, arranged neatly across quarters. A roadmap is useful. It shows intent and sequence. But it doesn't explain why those choices, and it rarely shows what was given up to make room for them. Consider two ways of presenting the same cloud program. The first says: "Migrate 80% of workloads to the cloud by the end of next year." It is clear and measurable. It is also silent on why, and it invites teams to lift and shift whatever is easiest to hit the number, including systems that gain nothing from moving. The second says: "Our product teams currently wait weeks for environments, and our peak-season capacity costs us heavily for capacity we use a few weeks a year. We will move the customer-facing and seasonal workloads first, because that's where elasticity and speed pay off. Stable back-office systems will stay where they are until there's a reason to move them." Same technology. Very different strategy. The second version makes a trade-off visible, and it gives teams a way to make good decisions without escalating every one of them. Choose the outcomes first I find it helpful to start every strategy conversation with a simple question: what needs to be different for the business in two years, and how will we know? Faster product change. Lower operational risk. Better customer experience. Stronger resilience. Lower cost to serve. These are outcomes. A new platform is only ever one possible means of achieving them. When strategy starts with technologies, it tends to measure adoption: how many workloads migrated, how many teams on the new platform. When it starts with outcomes, it measures change: lead time, incident rates, cost per transaction, customer effort. Adoption is easy to report. Change is what the business is paying for. Make the constraints explicit Every technology decision has costs, and the most dangerous ones are the costs nobody wrote down. Migration effort. Skills the organization doesn't yet have. Vendor dependency. Additional operating complexity. And, most often overlooked, opportunity cost: everything the same people could have been doing instead. A strong strategy puts these costs on the table rather than hiding them behind a target-state diagram. It is uncomfortable, because it makes it obvious that not everything can be done. That discomfort is the point. I've found that a simple one-page view for each major initiative, covering the outcome, the investment, the people it needs, what it will displace, and the risk if we don't do it, leads to far better conversations than any capability map. Three priorities, not fourteen When everything is strategic, nothing is. In my experience, very few organizations can genuinely execute more than three transformational priorities at the same time. The constraint usually isn't money. It's the limited number of people who understand the business, the systems, and how to lead change, and the leadership attention needed to unblock the hard parts. A credible strategy identifies the few changes that will create disproportionate value and protects the capacity to deliver them. Everything else is either business as usual, deliberately deferred, or stopped. That means some good ideas won't get funded this year. I believe that's not a failure of the strategy. It's evidence that the strategy is working. Define what you will stop doing This is the part most strategies leave out, and I think it's the most valuable. Organizations are very good at adding technology and remarkably poor at removing it. Every acquisition, every urgent project, and every enthusiastic team leaves something behind. Over time, the estate fills with overlapping tools, bespoke integrations, and systems that nobody wants to own but everybody is afraid to switch off. I've seen an environment running four separate monitoring tools, each introduced for a sensible reason at the time. Incidents routinely involved four teams looking at four dashboards, each with part of the picture. Consolidating them wasn't exciting work, and it never appeared on a strategy slide. But it reduced incident resolution time more than any new tool would have. A rule I'd like to see in more strategies: every new platform should come with a named retirement. If we are introducing something, we should be explicit about what it replaces, by when, and who is accountable for switching the old one off. Simplification doesn't happen as a side effect. It has to be funded, tracked, and celebrated like any other delivery. Build where you differentiate, buy where you don't Build-versus-buy decisions are where strategy often becomes emotional. Building feels like control. Engineers enjoy it, and custom solutions fit the organization's processes precisely. But I've seen a team spend two years building an internal ticketing and workflow tool that, by the end, required six engineers just to keep running. A commercial product would have done 90% of what was needed from the start. My default is straightforward. If a capability is not the reason customers choose you, such as identity, HR, service management, or most internal tooling, buy it, configure it lightly, and adapt your processes where you can. Save your scarce engineering talent for the few things that genuinely make the business different. There are exceptions, of course. But they should be argued for, not assumed. My perspective: strategy is the courage to choose I have come to believe that the real test of a technology strategy is not how ambitious it sounds, but how clearly it says no. A good strategy helps an organization say yes with conviction to the few things that matter most. Just as importantly, it helps people say no, or not yet, without feeling that they are blocking progress, because the reasons were agreed in advance. There are contexts where this needs nuance. Early-stage and fast-growing organizations sometimes benefit from keeping options open rather than committing too hard, too early. Some regulated industries genuinely need redundancy that would look wasteful elsewhere. Those are real considerations. But they are specific situations with specific reasons, not a general excuse to avoid choosing. My view: technology strategy is the discipline of trade-offs. Choose the outcomes, make the costs visible, limit the priorities, and be explicit about what you will stop. If a strategy can't do that, it isn't finished yet. A roadmap tells people what you'll do. A strategy tells them what you won't, and why.
